title: 05. Load Balancing & Scalability: Layer 4 Load Balancer
summary: A Layer 4 load balancer operates at the OSI transport layer (TCP/UDP), distributing connections based solely on IP address, port, and protocol — without inspecting the application payload — making it extremely fast and…
objectives: What information does a Layer 4 load balancer use to make routing decisions, and what does it deliberately ignore?
Explain NAT mode vs. Direct Server Return (DSR) and when you would choose each.
Why is L4 called "protocol-agnostic," and what are some real-world protocols it load-balances that L7 cannot?
What state does an L4 load balancer hold, and what happens to active connections if the balancer crashes?

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** A Layer 4 load balancer operates at the OSI transport layer (TCP/UDP), distributing connections based solely on IP address, port, and protocol — without inspecting the application payload — making it extremely fast and lightweight but unable to make content-aware routing decisions.

A Layer 4 (L4) load balancer makes its routing decision using only the information available in the IP and TCP/UDP headers: source IP, source port, destination IP (the virtual IP), destination port, and the protocol number. It does **not** parse HTTP, gRPC, TLS SNI, or any application-layer bytes — by the time the first packet of payload arrives, the L4 balancer has already picked a backend and either NAT'd the connection or forwarded it via Direct Server Return. The benefit of this blindness is raw speed: an L4 balancer can be implemented as a packet processor that touches each packet only once, rewriting five fields (src/dst IP+port and checksum) in nanoseconds, with no per-connection parsing overhead. Google's Maglev, the software L4 balancer that fronts Google's entire ingress, sustains tens of millions of packets per second per node and is the canonical proof that software L4 can match bespoke hardware.

The **first** reason L4 dominates high-throughput ingress is **throughput**. An L7 balancer like NGINX must terminate the TCP connection, read the HTTP request line and headers, decide a route, then establish a new TCP connection to the backend and forward — two connections in flight per client request, plus parsing overhead. An L4 balancer simply rewrites the destination IP and forwards the same packets, maintaining the illusion of a single TCP connection from client to backend. This is **Network Address Translation (NAT) mode** — the canonical implementation, used by Linux Virtual Server (IPVS), HAProxy in TCP mode, and AWS Network Load Balancer. The connection table is per-flow state, looked up by 5-tuple, and the data path is a handful of memory accesses. AWS NLB handles millions of connections per second per listener precisely because it does this and nothing else; if it had to parse HTTP it would be 5–10× slower.

The **second** reason is **protocol agnosticism**. Because L4 never looks at the payload, it works for any TCP or UDP protocol — HTTP, HTTPS, gRPC, MQTT, SMTP, database wire protocols, Kafka's binary protocol, Redis's RESP, Cassandra's native transport. The same AWS NLB can front an HTTPS web tier in the morning and a Kafka broker pool in the afternoon; the same HAProxy in TCP mode can load-balance Redis writes and MySQL reads without reconfiguration. This matters in real systems: Netflix's Cassandra clusters sit behind L4 balancers because Cassandra's binary protocol has no HTTP equivalent; Uber's Kafka brokers use L4 (AWS NLB) because the Kafka client needs direct TCP to a specific broker for partition leadership. An L7 balancer simply cannot handle these protocols — there is no HTTP request to route on.

The **third** reason is **connection persistence**. Once an L4 balancer picks a backend for a TCP connection, every packet on that connection goes to the same backend until the connection closes (or times out). This is critical for stateful protocols — PostgreSQL's wire protocol authenticates once and reuses the connection for thousands of queries; SSH sessions, MQTT subscriptions, WebSocket upgrades all rely on every packet landing on the same backend. L7 balancers, by contrast, can route each HTTP request independently (a feature called "multiplexing"), which is great for stateless APIs but breaks for stateful protocols. The L4 model is: one connection, one backend, period — which is also why L4 is the right choice for any database proxy, message broker front-end, or long-lived streaming protocol.

A powerful variant is **Direct Server Return (DSR)**, also called "half-NAT" or "return-asymmetric routing." In DSR mode, the balancer forwards the client's request packet to the backend (rewriting only the destination MAC, not the IP), and the backend responds **directly** to the client — bypassing the balancer entirely on the return path. The backend accomplishes this by configuring the VIP as a local loopback address and using it as the source IP on the response. The benefit: the balancer's egress bandwidth is freed up, because it only handles the (typically smaller) request, not the (typically much larger) response. This is how video streaming services scale: a single Netflix Open Connect box can serve gigabits per second of video egress, but the balancer only sees the small HTTP range request that initiated the stream. DSR is widely used at CDNs, video platforms, and large-file download services where response bandwidth dwarfs request bandwidth.

The trade-off is the loss of **content awareness**. Because L4 does not parse the payload, it cannot route `/api/*` to one backend and `/static/*` to another; it cannot terminate TLS (it can pass-through TLS, but cannot read SNI to route by hostname — though modern L4+ balancers like AWS NLB do support SNI-based TLS listener config); it cannot rewrite headers, inject cookies, or compress responses. If you need any of these, you must put an L7 balancer behind the L4 balancer — a common two-tier architecture where an L4 (NLB) handles the raw TCP throughput and an L7 (ALB, NGINX, Envoy) handles the HTTP logic. AWS explicitly recommends this for the highest-throughput HTTPS sites: NLB terminates the TCP, fans out to a fleet of NGINX or ALB instances, and those handle TLS termination and HTTP routing. The L4 does what it's good at (millions of connections), the L7 does what it's good at (HTTP-aware routing).

Real-world examples are everywhere. **AWS NLB** is the canonical managed L4 — operating at millions of connections per second, sub-millisecond latency overhead, used by virtually every RDS Multi-AZ read replica, every Kafka-on-MSK cluster, every gaming backend. **HAProxy in TCP mode** is the open-source default — Netflix uses it for internal TCP services, and it can hit hundreds of thousands of connections per box. **Google Maglev** is the in-house software L4 that fronts every Google service (Search, YouTube, Gmail) — documented in a 2016 paper, running on commodity Linux servers, using a consistent-hash packet distribution that survives node failure with minimal connection disruption. **IPVS** (Linux Virtual Server) is the kernel-level L4 used inside Kubernetes for `kube-proxy` in IPVS mode — capable of routing hundreds of thousands of service-level packets per second. **Envoy** can run as L4 (TCP proxy mode) and is the default sidecar in Istio for raw TCP passthrough.

The failure modes of L4 are subtle. Because the balancer holds per-connection state, a balancer crash can drop every active connection — which is why production L4 deployments use connection sync between redundant pairs (Conntrackd, keepalived's `lvs_sync_daemon`), so the standby inherits the connection table on failover. UDP adds another wrinkle: there is no "connection" in the protocol, so the balancer must use source-IP+port hashing to maintain a flow-to-backend mapping with a timeout, and a hash collision can misroute. TLS pass-through prevents the balancer from inspecting or terminating certificates, which is fine for self-contained backends but blocks central certificate management. And because L4 cannot see HTTP errors, it cannot do per-request outlier detection — it relies on TCP-level signals (RST, timeout) for health, which are slower to detect than an HTTP 500. These trade-offs are why L4 and L7 coexist in nearly every production architecture: L4 at the front door for raw throughput, L7 behind it for content logic.

The client opens a TCP connection to the service's virtual IP (VIP) — for example, `203.0.113.10:443`. The L4 balancer owns the VIP and accepts the SYN. 2. The balancer consults its connection table — keyed by the 5-tuple (src_ip, src_port, dst_ip, dst_port, protocol) — and applies its algorithm (often consistent hashing on src_ip, or simple round-robin per new flow) to pick a backend, e.g. `10.0.1.5:443`. 3. In NAT mode, the balancer rewrites the destination IP/port to the chosen backend and forwards the SYN; the backend replies to the balancer, which rewrites the source back to the VIP and forwards to the client. Every subsequent packet on this flow uses the same backend — the connection is sticky. 4. In DSR mode, the balancer rewrites only the destination MAC (not the IP) and forwards the packet to the backend; the backend, which has the VIP configured as a loopback alias, sends the response directly to the client, bypassing the balancer entirely on the return path. 5. The balancer maintains the connection entry in its table until it observes a FIN/RST or an idle timeout fires — typically 30–60 seconds for TCP. Health checks are TCP-level (connection success) or application-protocol-agnostic probes, since the balancer cannot interpret the payload.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- L4 health check: just open a TCP connect to the backend.
- NAT-style TCP load balancer with a 5-tuple connection table.
- Bidirectionally copy bytes between two sockets.
- Mock Layer 4 load balancer using sockets.
- Demonstrates: VIP accept, 5-tuple connection table, NAT-style forwarding,
- Round-robin and source-IP-hash selection, and a TCP health check.
- NOTE: this is a teaching mock. Real L4 LBs are kernel-level (IPVS, eBPF/XDP).
- Running this requires root to bind low ports; use 8080 instead.

**Defines:** `Backend`, `Layer4LoadBalancer`

```python
# Mock Layer 4 load balancer using sockets.
# Demonstrates: VIP accept, 5-tuple connection table, NAT-style forwarding,
# round-robin and source-IP-hash selection, and a TCP health check.
# NOTE: this is a teaching mock. Real L4 LBs are kernel-level (IPVS, eBPF/XDP).
#       Running this requires root to bind low ports; use 8080 instead.

import socket
import threading
import time
import hashlib
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Backend:
    host: str
    port: int
    healthy: bool = True
    _last_check: float = 0.0

    def tcp_health_check(self, timeout: float = 1.0) -> bool:
        """L4 health check: just open a TCP connect to the backend."""
        try:
            with socket.create_connection((self.host, self.port), timeout=timeout):
                self.healthy = True
        except OSError:
            self.healthy = False
        self._last_check = time.time()
        return self.healthy

class Layer4LoadBalancer:
    """NAT-style TCP load balancer with a 5-tuple connection table."""

    def __init__(self, listen_host: str, listen_port: int,
                 backends: list[Backend], algorithm: str = "rr"):
        self.listen_host = listen_host
        self.listen_port = listen_port
        self.backends = backends
        self.algorithm = algorithm
        self._rr_idx = 0
        self._lock = threading.Lock()
        # Connection table: 5-tuple -> backend (sticky per flow)
        self._flow_table: dict[tuple, Backend] = {}
        self._hc_stop = threading.Event()

    # ----- selection algorithms -----
    def _pick(self, src_ip: str, src_port: int) -> Backend | None:
        healthy = [b for b in self.backends if b.healthy]
        if not healthy:
            return None
        if self.algorithm == "hash":
            # Source-IP hash: same client -> same backend (affinity)
            h = int(hashlib.md5(src_ip.encode()).hexdigest(), 16)
            return healthy[h % len(healthy)]
        else:  # round-robin
            with self._lock:
                b = healthy[self._rr_idx % len(healthy)]
                self._rr_idx += 1
            return b

    # ----- health-check loop -----
    def _health_loop(self):
        while not self._hc_stop.wait(5.0):
            for b in self.backends:
                was = b.healthy
                now = b.tcp_health_check()
                if was != now:
                    print(f"[HC] {b.host}:{b.port} -> {'OK' if now else 'DOWN'}")

    # ----- the core: NAT a TCP connection -----
    def _pipe(self, src: socket.socket, dst: socket.socket):
        """Bidirectionally copy bytes between two sockets."""
        try:
            while True:
                data = src.recv(65536)
                if not data:
                    break
                dst.sendall(data)
        except OSError:
            pass
        finally:
            try: src.shutdown(socket.SHUT_RD)
            except OSError: pass
            try: dst.shutdown(socket.SHUT_WR)
            except OSError: pass
            src.close(); dst.close()

    def _handle_client(self, client_sock: socket.socket, client_addr):
        src_ip, src_port = client_addr[0], client_addr[1]
        flow = (src_ip, src_port, self.listen_host, self.listen_port, "tcp")
        # Sticky: reuse existing flow assignment if present
        backend = self._flow_table.get(flow)
        if backend is None or not backend.healthy:
            backend = self._pick(src_ip, src_port)
            if backend is None:
                client_sock.close()
                return
            self._flow_table[flow] = backend

        try:
            upstream = socket.create_connection((backend.host, backend.port), timeout=2.0)
        except OSError:
            backend.healthy = False
            client_sock.close()
            return

        print(f"[L4] {src_ip}:{src_port} -> {backend.host}:{backend.port}")
        # Two threads: client->backend and backend->client (NAT both ways)
        threading.Thread(target=self._pipe, args=(client_sock, upstream), daemon=True).start()
        threading.Thread(target=self._pipe, args=(upstream, client_sock), daemon=True).start()

    def run(self):
        self._hc_thread = threading.Thread(target=self._health_loop, daemon=True)
        self._hc_thread.start()
        srv = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
        srv.setsockopt(socket.SOL_SOCKET, socket.SO_REUSEADDR, 1)
        srv.bind((self.listen_host, self.listen_port))
        srv.listen(128)
        print(f"[L4] listening on {self.listen_host}:{self.listen_port} "
              f"(algo={self.algorithm}, backends={len(self.backends)})")
        while True:
            client, addr = srv.accept()
            threading.Thread(target=self._handle_client, args=(client, addr),
                             daemon=True).start()

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Demo: front three "backends" on ports 9001/9002/9003.
    # In a real test you'd start three echo servers on those ports first.
    backends = [
        Backend("127.0.0.1", 9001),
        Backend("127.0.0.1", 9002),
        Backend("127.0.0.1", 9003),
    ]
    lb = Layer4LoadBalancer("0.0.0.0", 8080, backends, algorithm="rr")
    lb.run()
```

quiz.explanation: A Layer 4 balancer uses only the OSI transport-layer header: source IP, source port, destination IP (the VIP), destination port, and protocol number (TCP or UDP) — collectively the "5-tuple." It deliberately ignores everything above layer 4: the HTTP method, URL path, headers, cookies, TLS SNI, request body, and response codes are all invisible.

quiz.question: Explain NAT mode vs. Direct Server Return (DSR) and when you would choose each.
options: Either works, but the requirements differ.
Choose L4 when: (1) you need raw throughput measured in millions of connections/sec or tens of Gbps; (2) the protocol is not HTTP — database, message broker, MQTT,…

quiz.explanation: In NAT mode, the balancer rewrites both directions of the connection: client→backend packets have their destination IP changed from VIP to backend IP, and backend→client replies have their source IP changed back to VIP. Both directions traverse the balancer, so the balancer's bandwidth must handle the sum of request and response traffic.

quiz.explanation: TLS termination requires parsing the TLS handshake — specifically, reading the ClientHello's SNI (Server Name Indication) field to know which certificate to present, then performing the cryptographic exchange to decrypt subsequent application data. That requires reading layer 7 bytes inside the TCP stream, which an L4 balancer by definition does not do.
